shaCheck: The head every proof names, 35faab4eeace3d7c9906085e7bb9d3c68980b8e1, was resolved before this handoff was pushed and in both places, because the two failures differ: `jj log -r 35faab4eeace3d7c9906085e7bb9d3c68980b8e1` in this workspace and `gh api repos/sjawhar/legion/commits/35faab4eeace3d7c9906085e7bb9d3c68980b8e1` on GitHub, each answering the same forty characters and the same subject, `Give each run its own name, so a wait cannot answer about a corpse`, which is the commit I drove.

implementerProof.how: I drove every shape rather than confirming the implementer's numbers, as last round: the substitution checked on the manifests the page publishes, parsed rather than read; three back-to-back re-runs; the delete-issued-while-Running shape; the ten-second paused shape; and the fixed-name control at this same head, which reproduces the defect the remedy removes. The waits were bounded at five seconds wherever a pass could otherwise come from the corpse having already gone. The claim the architect singled out — that the Service carries no literal name, so a selector left behind is impossible rather than merely checked — holds on the published text: four placeholder sites, all filled by the one substitution, and the Service's selector equal to the Job's name.

proof.criterion: The rename reaches everywhere: no literal name survives the substitution, and the Service that results selects the pods the Job will make.
proof.surface: The two manifests as the page publishes them, extracted by script rather than retyped, run through the sequence's own `sed`, then parsed; and live admission for the filled Job.
proof.command: a script lifting both yaml blocks out of the section ; `sed -e "s|<workload>|$workload|g"` on each, exactly as the sequence writes it ; a YAML parse asserting the Job's `metadata.name`, the Service's `metadata.name`, its `ownerReferences[0].name` and its `spec.selector['job-name']` ; then kubectl apply --dry-run=server on the filled Job
proof.observed: Four placeholder sites, one in the Job and three in the Service, and the single global substitution fills all four: zero occurrences of the placeholder remain in either file, and the Service's name, its owner reference's name and its `selector: {job-name: …}` all equal the run's name, which is what the Job controller stamps on its own pods. The filled Job is accepted server-side with nothing created. So a Service pointing at nothing is not a thing a role can produce by forgetting a site; there is no second site to forget.
proof.negativeControl: The failure mode this guards against is the one that reads like the label failure, so I checked it by its symptom rather than by its text: a Service whose selector did not follow the rename would select no pod, and the selector I parsed selects exactly the label the Job sets — which I also measured on a live pod, whose `job-name` label is the run's name.

proof.criterion: The re-run shapes: a wait cannot answer about a corpse once each run has its own name.
proof.surface: The live namespace from this role container, six Jobs, each bounded at a fifteen-minute deadline and a five-minute cleanup window and deleted by hand.
proof.command: three back-to-back re-runs, each `apply` → `--for=create --timeout=120s` → `--for=condition=Ready --timeout=5s`, counting the pods each selector matches and whether it matches the previous run's ; a run taken to Ready and then deleted **while Running**, followed at once by a fresh run ; the ten-second paused shape ; and the same two-run shape under a fixed name as the control
proof.observed: Every run matched exactly one pod — its own. In the three back-to-back re-runs `--for=create` returned 0 at six seconds each time, the five-second Ready wait named that same pod (timing out as a bounded wait should while the pod was still starting), and each new run's selector matched the previous run's corpse **zero** times. The delete-while-Running shape is the same: the second run's selector matched one pod and the first run's matched none, and its Ready wait named the new pod and was met. The paused shape: create at 10 s, one pod matched, Ready at 11 s, Postgres's own `database system is ready to accept connections` after it. The control at this head shows what the remedy removes: under a fixed name the selector matched **two** pods at once, one `Terminating` and one `Pending`, and the five-second Ready wait answered `condition met` for both.
proof.negativeControl: The five-second bound is the control rather than a convenience: a remedy that only worked once the previous pod had gone would pass a generous wait and fail this one, and in the three back-to-back runs the corpse was still there — the control proves it, since the same shape under a fixed name found two pods in that window.

proof.criterion: The suffix does what the paragraph claims: two names built in the same second differ, and the name is unique enough for the use.
proof.surface: The sequence's own name-building command, run here.
proof.command: ten runs of `python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(3))'` in one second ; then twenty thousand draws counted
proof.observed: The ten differ. Twenty thousand draws gave 19,991 distinct values with a maximum repeat of two, which is what a three-byte random suffix is: 16.7 million values, collision-free for the handful of runs an issue makes, and random rather than guaranteed. Recorded as what it is rather than as a guarantee the paragraph does not claim.
proof.negativeControl: The cross-role case the architect asked about is the same measurement: two names built in the same second from the same command differ, so two role containers of one pod starting together cannot take one name.

proof.criterion: The new text read as a reader meets it, in both orders, and the regression over what earlier rounds proved.
proof.surface: The page at this head, and the branch's whole diff against its fork point.
proof.command: a reading of the naming paragraph, the sequence and the label bullet in both orders ; a grep of every added line of the diff for the four private names, each read in context
proof.observed: The two halves of the naming rule agree wherever a reader starts: the paragraph says the name is built once at the top of the sequence and substituted into both manifests, and the sequence does exactly that in its first three lines; the Job's comment says the substitution reaches the Service too, and it does. No private name is added anywhere: the compute-class selector, the scratch storage class and the admission policy appear in no added line, and the namespace's literal matches three times, each the ordinary English word in prose — twice in the guidance, once quoted inside the implement handoff.
